title: How to Calculate Your Salary Australia: Hourly to Annual with Award and Minimum Wage Rates
description: Convert your hourly rate to an annual salary in Australia. Learn the formula, National Minimum Wage, award rates, casual loading, super, and tax for 2026-27.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the National Minimum Wage and an award rate?
faqs.a: The National Minimum Wage ($26.44 per hour from 1 July 2026) is the base rate for employees not covered by an award or agreement. Award rates are higher minimums set for specific industries and occupations, found in pay guides from the Fair Work Ombudsman. Most employees are covered by an award, so their minimum pay is likely above the National Minimum Wage.

faqs.q: How do I calculate my annual salary from my hourly rate?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work each week, then by 52. For a standard full-time role of 38 hours per week: annual gross = hourly rate × 38 × 52. This gives a base figure before adding casual loading, penalties, or allowances. Use the timesheet on this site to do the calculation automatically.

No. Superannuation is paid on top of your salary. From 1 July 2026, the Super Guarantee is 12% of your ordinary time earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. Your advertised salary or hourly rate does not include super; it is an additional cost to your employer.

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding Your Salary Australia: From Hourly to Annual

When you see a job ad quoting an hourly rate or an annual salary, it helps to know how the two relate. In Australia, the standard full-time week is 38 hours, and the basic formula to convert an hourly rate to annual gross pay is:

**Annual gross ≈ hourly rate × hours per week × 52**

This article explains that formula, the role of the National Minimum Wage, award rates, casual loading, superannuation, and tax. Whether you are negotiating a job offer or checking your current pay, understanding these components gives you a clearer picture of your **salary Australia**.

### The National Minimum Wage vs Award Rates

From 1 July 2026, the Fair Work Commission set the National Minimum Wage at $26.44 per hour, which equals $1,004.90 per week for a 38-hour week. This is the legal floor for employees who are not covered by an award or registered agreement. Casual employees get a 25% loading on top, making the casual minimum $33.05 per hour.

However, most Australian employees are covered by an award. Awards are industry- or occupation-specific documents that set higher minimum pay rates, penalty rates, allowances, and other conditions. The Fair Work Ombudsman publishes pay guides for each award. For example, a retail employee or a hospitality worker will likely have a minimum hourly rate above the National Minimum Wage. Always check the relevant award to know your correct minimum.

If you are award-free, the National Minimum Wage applies. If you are covered by an enterprise agreement, that agreement may set different rates, but they cannot be less than the award.

### Converting Hourly to Annual: The 38-Hour Assumption

When converting an hourly rate to an annual figure, we assume a consistent 38-hour week, 52 weeks per year. This is the standard for full-time employment in Australia. The formula is:

**Annual gross = hourly rate × 38 × 52**

For example, an hourly rate of $30.00 gives an annual gross of $30 × 38 × 52 = $59,280. If you work part-time or casual, your weekly hours may vary. The [the timesheet](/) on this site lets you enter your base hourly rate and optionally add casual loading to see your annual, fortnightly, and weekly figures.

### Casual Loading and Penalty Rates

Casual employees receive a 25% loading on top of the base hourly rate to compensate for not receiving paid leave entitlements. If you are casual, your effective hourly rate is higher. The checkbox on the timesheet adds this loading automatically. Never enter a rate that already includes casual loading; the tool adds it for you.

Penalty rates (for weekends, public holidays, late nights) and allowances are not included in the simple annual conversion. They are additional payments that depend on when and where you work. For a precise estimate, refer to your award's pay guide [pay guides](/blog) or use the Fair Work Ombudsman’s Pay and Conditions Tool.

### Superannuation: Paid on Top

Superannuation is not part of your salary; it is an extra payment your employer makes into your super fund. From 1 July 2026, the Super Guarantee is 12% of your ordinary time earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. So if your annual gross salary is $60,000, your employer must contribute an additional $7,200 into super. This is not deducted from your pay. When comparing job offers, remember that super is on top of the quoted salary. See [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) for more.

### Tax and Medicare Levy

Your annual gross salary is not what you take home. The Australian Taxation Office applies progressive tax rates for 2026–27:

- Nil on the first $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

In addition, most residents pay a Medicare levy of 2% (with reductions for low-income earners). The [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) page on this site estimates your net income after tax and Medicare, using the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds (as 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed). Note that HELP repayments, the Medicare levy surcharge, and salary packaging are not included in this estimate.

### Fortnightly and Weekly Breakdown

Knowing your fortnightly pay is useful for budgeting, especially if you are paid every two weeks. Simply multiply your weekly gross by 2. For a $30/hour rate on 38 hours:

- Weekly: $30 × 38 = $1,140
- Fortnightly: $1,140 × 2 = $2,280
- Annual: $1,140 × 52 = $59,280

The timesheet shows these figures automatically.

### Average Earnings in Australia

For context, the Australian Bureau of Statistics reported in May 2026 that full-time adult average weekly ordinary time earnings were $2,083.70, and total earnings for all employees (including part-time) were $1,579.20 per week. These figures are higher than the National Minimum Wage because they include higher-paid roles. Use [average pay](/topics/average-pay) to compare your rate to national averages.

### Putting It All Together

To calculate your own **salary Australia**:

1. Find your base hourly rate (check your award or agreement).
2. Decide your weekly hours (38 for full-time, fewer for part-time).
3. Multiply hourly × hours × 52 for annual gross.
4. Add 25% if you are casual (the timesheet does this).
5. Remember super is on top (12% of ordinary earnings).
6. Estimate tax and Medicare using the [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) tool.

This gives you a solid estimate, but always consult your employer, the Fair Work Ombudsman, or a qualified adviser for your specific situation. The [reference tables](/data) on this site provide quick lookups for minimum rates and tax brackets.

### Important Disclaimer

Annual pay shown here is hourly rate × hours per week × 52. It assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, no allowances, and no salary sacrifice. Super is estimated at 12% of ordinary earnings only, paid on top, and stops at the $270,830 maximum contribution base. Tax is the 2026–27 resident scale with the full tax-free threshold. Medicare uses the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds because the 2026–27 reduction thresholds were not confirmed here. HELP, the Medicare levy surcharge, and salary packaging are not deducted. This is an estimate, not a determination of your pay or tax.
